attacks.claim: The public Recent signers panel renders the signer's full name and postal code, contradicting the agreed rule of first name, last initial and city at most. The output is cached at the CDN and public, so the exposure of political-petition signers' identities is hard to undo.
attacks.evidence:
• {{ s.full_name }} {{ s.city }} {{ s.postal_code }}
    • vs. 'public signer lists may show at most first name, last initial and city'

attacks.claim: Publishing full names and postal codes of EU signers, who are signing a political petition (special-category-adjacent political opinion data), violates GDPR data minimisation and the agreed display constraint.

The newsletter consent checkbox is pre-ticked, which is not valid GDPR consent. It also bundles 'other campaigns' from the organizer, so it is not specific. Organizer CSV exports are built from this invalid consent.

Validation errors are conveyed only by border and background colour. The aria-live error paragraph is never populated, and there is no aria-invalid or aria-describedby. This fails WCAG 2.1 AA (1.4.1, 3.3.1), which was agreed as required for public flows.
The client handles only 422 and ok responses. A 409 duplicate, 5xx or network failure produces no feedback at all, so the user is left on a form that appears to do nothing.
attacks.evidence: if (res.status === 422) {...} if (res.ok) window.location = ... ABSENT: handling for 409/5xx/network errors

attacks.claim: The sign endpoint has no described CSRF protection, bot protection or rate limiting. Attackers can mass-create signatures to inflate the public counts. Each signature also sends a confirmation email to an arbitrary address, which enables email bombing of third parties and damages Postmark sender reputation.
attacks.evidence: <form ... method="post" novalidate> ABSENT: CSRF token, CAPTCHA, rate limit, per-address email quota

attacks.claim: No retention period is defined for confirmed signatures (email, postal code), and no erasure or withdrawal path exists for signers, so GDPR storage limitation and data-subject rights are unaddressed.
attacks.evidence: ABSENT: retention period for confirmed signatures, erasure/withdrawal process

attacks.claim: Rollback only swaps the sign form back to the Follow button. It does not unpublish already-exposed PII in the Recent signers panel or its cached copies. A privacy exposure is therefore not reversible through the stated path.
attacks.evidence: Rollback: flip `petitions_signing` off; sign form is replaced by the existing "Follow this petition" button.

attacks.claim: The accessibility claim relies on an automated axe-core scan of the sign page only. It does not cover error states, keyboard use or screen-reader behaviour, so it does not demonstrate WCAG 2.1 AA conformance. QA also never caught the PII panel mismatch.
attacks.evidence: axe-core automated scan on sign page | 0 violations

attacks.claim: EU signer emails go to Postmark, a US vendor, and the artifact cites only a DPA without naming a transfer mechanism or fallback provider. EU residency is inferred from postal code.
attacks.evidence: Confirmation emails go through Postmark; DPA countersigned 2026-09-14

attacks.claim: The 409 duplicate response lets anyone test whether a given email has signed a petition.
The submit button is not disabled while the request is in flight, so double-clicks can post twice.
Load testing covers sign writes only. It does not cover 15s polling of live counts across many petition pages, which is the read-heavy hot path.
Monitoring covers only submit error rate and bounce rate, with no alerting on purge job failure or export anomalies.
attacks.evidence: Watch `sign_submit_error_rate` (< 0.5%) and confirmation email bounce rate (< 2%)
